Its history goes back at least to the Tang dynasty, and it may have come in from the northwest. It was then used mainly in popular entertainment music (san'yue), and by the Five Dynasties period it is also recorded in court music.

拍板的音色具有明亮、清脆的特質，具有強烈的穿透力。其音響特徵因材質而異：木製拍板: The paiban's timbre is bright and clear, with strong carrying power. Its sound differs with the material: a wooden paiban has a warm timbre full of character, with a mellow quality, while a metal one is sharp and bright and rings out pleasingly. The paiban is a percussion instrument of the high register, with a fairly narrow range and no wide variation in pitch. Its resonance comes mostly from direct impact: the sound bursts out at once and decays quickly. Compared with the deep, round tone of drums, its timbre is crisper and more forceful; compared with gongs and cymbals, its sound is finer and more precise, with a stronger sense of rhythm. This distinct percussive timbre makes it an ideal rhythm instrument in the accompaniment of narrative singing and music drama, where it effectively sets the mood of a performance.

It appears in narrative singing and in music drama such as Peking opera, Kunqu and Yue opera, and also in instrumental line-ups such as Jiangnan sizhu, Chaozhou xianshi, Sunan chuida, nanguan, shifan luogu and the eight suites of Shanxi. When listening, notice the short beats produced by striking the several pieces of hardwood or bamboo together.

The paiban is an idiophone in Chinese music, Hornbostel–Sachs 111.11. It is made of several flat pieces of hardwood or bamboo, ivory or metal also being used in the past, loosely bound together at one end with cord. The player holds it in one hand and strikes it vertically, producing a clear clapping sound. It is often called guban together with the small drum, one player holding the clapper in one hand and the drumstick in the other, and is used in narrative singing and in Peking opera, Kunqu, Cantonese opera and the like; it is also found in instrumental line-ups such as Jiangnan sizhu, Chaozhou xiyue, Sunan chuida, nanguan, shifan luogu and the eight suites of Shanxi.

隨著時代發展，拍板逐漸成為民間說唱音樂、器樂與戲曲伴奏的重要工具，廣泛應用於「板: As time went on the paiban became an important tool in the accompaniment of popular narrative singing, instrumental music and music drama, widely used in 'clapper' storytelling, Yuan dynasty zaju, nanguan music and many other art forms. The design of the paiban differs greatly between regions and genres, producing a variety of playing styles. Shandong kuaishu uses metal clappers, with a clear, bright timbre; the northern kuaiban shu and lianhualuo use a set of seven wooden pieces, the 'seven pieces', whose complex combined striking technique creates rich rhythmic effects, showing how important and how widely used the paiban is in Chinese traditional music.
